title: Array Indexing
description: What is the time complexity of accessing an array element by its index?
explanation: Index access is O(1): the array computes the location of a slot directly rather than scanning earlier elements. This assumes constant-cost indexing into a conventional array.

title: Array Insertion
description: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array?
explanation: Inserting at the beginning requires shifting up to n existing elements to make room, so the worst-case time is O(n). A dynamic array may also need to resize.

title: Array Traversal
description: How many elements are visited when traversing an array of size n exactly once?
explanation: A complete traversal visits each of the n elements once, so exactly n elements are visited. There is no nested traversal in this operation.

title: Big O Notation
description: What does Big O notation commonly describe in algorithm analysis?
explanation: Big O describes an asymptotic upper bound on growth as input size increases. It does not give exact runtime in seconds, and the input case being analyzed must be stated separately.

title: Nested Loops
description: Two nested loops each execute n times. What is their total time complexity?
explanation: If each loop executes n times for every iteration of its enclosing loop, the body runs n times n, or n squared times. With constant-cost body work, the total is O(n^2).

title: Logarithmic Complexity
description: An algorithm repeatedly halves its input size. What is its typical time complexity?
explanation: Repeated halving reaches a constant size after about log base 2 of n steps. With constant work per step, the typical running time is O(log n); halving alone does not bound additional work done at each step.

title: Linear Search Basics
description: Which approach does linear search use?
explanation: Linear search checks elements sequentially until it finds the target or reaches the end. It does not require sorting, halving the search interval, or hashing.

title: Linear Search Worst Case
description: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
explanation: The target may be absent or at the last position, requiring up to n checks. Assuming constant-cost comparisons, this gives O(n) worst-case time.

title: Linear Search Best Case
description: When does linear search achieve its best-case time complexity?
explanation: If the target is the first element, linear search succeeds after one comparison, giving O(1) best-case time. A last or absent target requires scanning the sequence.

title: Binary Search Requirement
description: What condition is required for standard binary search?
explanation: Binary search needs sorted data so a comparison with the midpoint can safely rule out one half. Duplicate values, odd lengths, and negative values are all compatible with standard binary search.

title: Binary Search Complexity
description: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search?
explanation: Each comparison discards roughly half of the remaining sorted search interval. This gives O(log n) worst-case comparisons for constant-cost random access and comparisons.

title: Binary Search Midpoint
description: Why is mid = low + (high - low) // 2 often preferred over (low + high) // 2?
options: Prevents integer overflow in fixed-width integer types
explanation: In fixed-width integer types, low + high can overflow even when both valid nonnegative indices fit individually. low + (high - low) // 2 avoids that sum. Python integers are not limited to a fixed width.

title: Bubble Sort Comparison
description: Bubble sort primarily compares which elements?
explanation: Bubble sort compares adjacent elements and swaps out-of-order neighbors. A pass moves the largest remaining element toward the end of the unsorted region.

title: Bubble Sort Complexity
description: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort?
explanation: In the worst case bubble sort makes a quadratic number of comparisons across its passes, giving O(n^2) time. Early stopping improves the best case but does not remove this worst case.

title: Bubble Sort Optimization
description: What can an optimized bubble sort do if no swaps occur during a pass?
explanation: A complete pass with no swaps means every adjacent pair is already in order, so the whole sequence is sorted and the algorithm can stop. One swap-free comparison alone is not sufficient.

title: Merge Sort Strategy
description: Which algorithmic strategy is used by merge sort?
explanation: Merge sort uses divide and conquer: split the input into smaller halves, sort them recursively, then merge the sorted results. It does not solve this task through greedy choice or backtracking.

title: Merge Sort Complexity
description: What is the typical time complexity of merge sort?
explanation: Typical array merge sort has O(log n) levels of splitting and O(n) total merging work at each level, giving O(n log n) time under constant-cost comparisons.

title: Merge Sort Merge Step
description: What happens during the merge step of merge sort?
explanation: The merge step combines two already-sorted subarrays by repeatedly taking the smaller next element and then appending any remaining tail. Simply concatenating the halves is not generally sorted.

title: Recursion Base Case
description: Why is a base case important in recursion?
explanation: A base case returns an answer without another recursive call, preventing unbounded recursion when recursive steps move toward it. A base case alone is not enough if the recursive argument never approaches it.

title: Recursive Factorial
description: What is factorial(4)?
explanation: factorial(4) is 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24. Factorial multiplies the positive integers through n; it is not n squared or a repeated doubling operation.

title: Recursion Call Stack
description: Which data structure is used to manage recursive function calls?
explanation: A call stack keeps active function frames, including arguments and the point at which each call should resume. Returning from a call restores the most recent unfinished call, following last-in, first-out order.

title: Sorting Stability
description: What does stability mean in a sorting algorithm?
options: Preserves relative order of equal keys
explanation: A stable sort preserves the original relative order of records with equal keys. Stability does not imply linear time, constant memory, or the absence of comparisons.

title: Comparison Sorting
description: Which of the following is a comparison-based sorting algorithm?
explanation: Merge sort orders items by comparing keys while merging sorted halves. Counting and radix sorts instead exploit key representations; bucket sorting distributes keys into ranges and may use a comparison sort inside individual buckets.

title: In-place Sorting
description: What does in-place sorting generally mean?
options: Uses extra array of size n
explanation: In-place sorting generally uses O(1) auxiliary storage beyond the input. This describes memory usage, not runtime; some conventions allow a small recursion stack, so the convention should be stated.

title: Sorting Lower Bound
description: What is the worst-case lower bound for general comparison-based sorting?
explanation: General comparison sorting needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case: a binary decision tree must distinguish n factorial possible orders of distinct keys. Non-comparison methods with restricted keys use different assumptions.
